Retail replenishment connects sales expectations with stock, supplier conditions and spending decisions. This dissertation asks whether a small local large language model can help that process and what it adds beyond a capable numerical planner. It follows the progression of the supplied Gilbert thesis, while using a newly written retail narrative and the completed no-repair Ollama study as its empirical foundation.

The study uses thirty selected store–product series from M5 and thirty from FreshRetailNet-50K, called RetailNet in the graphs. Three language-model roles read current supplier messages, request a planning tool and review its checks. Two reference policies provide the comparisons: conventional ordering and the same structured-data planner without language-model roles. Two historical weeks, three operating situations and thirty simulation seeds produce 1,080 completed runs and 7,560 fresh model calls.

Compared with conventional ordering, the complete workflow increased simulated demand fulfilment by 25.28 percentage points in M5 and 0.78 points in RetailNet. The paired inventory operating-cost reductions were 70.34% and 4.52%. These measures concern a disclosed simulator and synthetic cost assumptions. They are not measured retailer profits or production savings.

The language model read all controlled supplier messages accurately. Business-priority selection was less reliable, especially during RetailNet promotions. The same numerical planner performed almost identically in M5 and slightly better in RetailNet, so it explains most of the inventory-performance improvement. The useful demonstrated LLM role is supplier-information interpretation within a bounded process; an additional numerical replenishment advantage was not established.

The experiments ran on Linux with four allocated CPU cores, 32 GiB memory and no GPU. Qwen2.5 1.5B was pretrained and served locally through Ollama, with no retail fine-tuning. LightGBM was fitted to past retail histories to supply the common forecast. The managerial recommendation is to retain a capable planner and explicit policy rules, then test language assistance where interpreting incoming information creates a real workload. Staff-time savings, implementation cost and commercial return remain questions for an operational pilot.
